title: Beer Before Liquor: Myth or Fact? What the Science Says
excerpt: Does "beer before liquor, never been sicker" hold up? A 2019 randomized crossover trial found drink order made no difference to hangovers. Here's what actually does: how much you drink, how fast, and congeners.
metaDescription: Is beer before liquor really worse? A 2019 crossover trial says drink order doesn't change your hangover. What does: total alcohol, pace, and congeners.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the order you drink in does not decide how bad your hangover will be. "Beer before liquor, never been sicker; liquor before beer, you're in the clear" is one of the most repeated drinking rules in the world, and the best test of it so far found no effect. In a 2019 randomized crossover trial run at Witten/Herdecke University in Germany and published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*, volunteers had nearly identical hangovers whether they drank beer first, wine first, or stuck to just one. What actually drives a hangover is how much alcohol you drink, how fast you drink it, and, to a lesser degree, what else comes along in the glass (the by-products called congeners). This guide explains the study, its limits, where the saying came from, and what genuinely makes a difference.

**The quick version you can use tonight:** count drinks, not drink types. Pace yourself to roughly one standard drink an hour or slower, alternate with water, eat before and while you drink, and lean toward clearer, lower-congener drinks if you're prone to bad hangovers. The sequence of beer, wine, and spirits is not something you need to plan around.

> **A note on safety.** This article explains general research about hangovers. It is not medical advice. Hangovers are a sign your body has processed more alcohol than it handles comfortably. If someone is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin, those can be signs of alcohol poisoning. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) and don't leave them alone. If you're regularly waking up hungover or worried about how much you drink, a doctor is a good, judgment-free place to start.

## Does "Beer Before Liquor" Actually Matter? What the Evidence Says

No. The order of drinks has no meaningful effect on hangover severity in the best evidence available. That's not a guess or a hunch. It's the specific question a German research team set out to test, and they designed the study carefully enough that the answer is worth taking seriously.

The rhyme makes a clear, testable prediction: two people who drink the same total amount of alcohol should feel different the next morning depending on which drink came first. If that were true, it should show up when you control the total amount and change only the order. When researchers did exactly that, the difference didn't appear.

What did predict a worse hangover was much more boring. People who reported feeling drunker, and people who vomited during the night, tended to have worse hangovers. Both of those are really markers of the same thing: more alcohol, absorbed faster, than the body handled well.

## Inside the 2019 Witten/Herdecke Crossover Trial

The study is often reported in headlines as "beer before wine doesn't matter," so it helps to know what was actually done.

### Who took part and what they drank

The trial was led by Jöran Köchling at Witten/Herdecke University, with colleagues including Kai Hensel of the University of Cambridge. It enrolled around 90 healthy volunteers aged roughly 19 to 40. The researchers split them into three groups:

1. **Beer first, then wine.** About two and a half pints of lager, followed by several large glasses of white wine.
2. **Wine first, then beer.** The same drinks in reverse order.
3. **Control groups.** Only beer or only wine, to the same target level of intoxication.

Drinks were served in measured amounts toward a set breath-alcohol target, so people in different groups ended the evening at a similar level of intoxication. Participants ate a standard meal beforehand, drank under supervision, and stayed overnight under medical observation.

### The crossover part

This is the clever bit. About a week later, everyone came back and did it again with the order switched. If you'd had beer-then-wine the first time, you got wine-then-beer the second time. (The single-drink controls switched to the other drink.)

A crossover design means each person is compared with themselves. That matters because hangover sensitivity varies hugely from person to person. Some people barely feel a night out; others are wrecked by a modest amount. By testing both orders in the same body, the study removes most of that noise.

### How hangovers were measured

The next day, participants rated their symptoms using a standard questionnaire called the Acute Hangover Scale, which scores things like thirst, fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea, stomach pain, and loss of appetite. The researchers also tracked factors like body weight, sex, drinking habits, and how drunk people said they felt.

### What they found

None of the drink orders produced a significantly different hangover from any other. Beer-then-wine, wine-then-beer, and beer-only or wine-only all came out about the same once total alcohol was held steady. The researchers' summary was blunt: the order of drinks doesn't seem to matter, and the folk wisdom doesn't hold up.

The factors that did line up with worse hangovers were self-rated drunkenness and vomiting. In plain terms, the more intoxicated you got, the worse you felt the next day. The study authors made the point that the real "warning signs" are feeling very drunk and being sick, not which glass came first.

### Why the study is fairly trustworthy

- **It was randomized**, so people didn't choose their own order.
- **It was a crossover**, so each person served as their own comparison.
- **Alcohol intake was controlled and measured**, instead of relying on people's memory of a night out.
- **It was published in a mainstream peer-reviewed nutrition journal**, the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*, in 2019.

## The Limits of the Study (and Why the Answer Still Holds)

No single study settles everything, and it's worth being honest about what this one didn't test.

**It tested beer and wine, not liquor.** The volunteers drank lager and white wine. The trial's title borrowed a different saying, "grape or grain but never the twain," which is about mixing wine and beer. So strictly speaking, it didn't put shots of vodka or whiskey after beer.

**The drinks were fairly low in congeners.** Lager and white wine are on the cleaner end. Mixing in dark spirits like bourbon or brandy brings more congeners, which can make hangovers worse for reasons that have nothing to do with order.

**It was a controlled lab night.** People ate a meal and drank in measured amounts under supervision. A real night out is messier.

**It involved young, healthy adults.** Results may differ for older people or people with health conditions.

Even with those limits, the underlying logic carries over to liquor. Once alcohol (ethanol) is in your bloodstream, your liver handles it the same way no matter whether it came from a pint, a glass of wine, or a shot. There's no known biological mechanism by which beer that arrived first makes liquor that arrived second more toxic. The things that plausibly differ between drinks, such as strength, carbonation, and congener content, matter regardless of order. Our [complete hangover science hub](/never-hungover/complete-hangover-science-hub-2025) goes deeper on the biology.

## Where "Beer Before Liquor, Never Been Sicker" Came From

Nobody knows exactly who first said it, and you should be wary of any article claiming a precise origin. What we can say is that versions of the rule exist in several languages, which suggests people in many drinking cultures noticed something and tried to put it into a rhyme.

- **English:** "Beer before liquor, never been sicker; liquor before beer, you're in the clear."
- **English (older):** "Grape or grain, but never the twain," a warning against mixing wine and beer at all.
- **German:** "Bier auf Wein, das lass sein; Wein auf Bier, das rat' ich dir," roughly "beer after wine, leave it be; wine after beer, I recommend it." Notice that the German rhyme says starting with beer is the safe choice, which is the opposite of what the English rhyme warns about beer first. When two folk rules point in opposite directions, that's a clue neither was based on chemistry.
- **Other languages:** similar order rhymes turn up in French and other European languages, often with different drinks swapped in.

### The theories people offer for why it caught on

Because there's no clear historical record, these are explanations, not established facts:

- **The pace theory (the most convincing one).** If you start with beer, you're drinking something weak, so you feel fine and keep going. By the time you switch to liquor, you've already had several drinks and your judgment is dulled, so you knock back strong drinks faster than you would have sober. The result is a lot of alcohol in a short window, and a brutal morning. Starting with liquor, on the other hand, gets you tipsy early, and then switching to beer slows you down. In both cases the order isn't the cause. It's a marker of how much and how fast you drank.
- **The "end of the night" theory.** In many settings, people drink beer early and move to shots or spirits late, when they're already drunk. The liquor gets blamed because it was the last thing they remember.
- **The social class theory.** Some writers suggest that in older European societies, beer was the drink of ordinary workers and wine the drink of wealthier people. Moving from wine to beer meant your night was going badly; moving from beer to wine meant things were looking up. This is plausible folklore, but it's hard to verify.
- **Memory bias.** People remember the nights that went badly. If you mixed drinks on a big night and felt terrible, you blame the mixing. You don't remember all the times you mixed and felt fine, or the nights you drank only beer and still felt awful.

The pace theory is the one worth keeping, because it points to something real you can change. The rhyme might be useful as a rough reminder not to speed up as the night goes on, but the order itself is not doing the damage.

## "Liquor Before Beer, You're in the Clear": Is That Version True?

No, not in the way it's usually meant. Drinking spirits first and beer second doesn't protect you from a hangover. If you drink the same total amount of alcohol in the same time frame, you'll get roughly the same hangover.

There is one grain of truth hidden in it. Starting with spirits often makes people feel the effects sooner, and some respond by slowing down. If switching to beer means you drink less alcohol per hour for the rest of the night, you may well wake up feeling better. But that's because of lower total intake and slower pace, not because liquor went in first. Someone who has five shots and then six beers in three hours is not "in the clear."

## Is Mixing Alcohol Bad? The Real Risks of Mixing Drinks

"Mixing drinks makes you sicker" is a close cousin of the beer-before-liquor rule. The research suggests that mixing types of alcohol is not harmful in itself. The 2019 trial found no worse hangovers in the mixed groups than in the single-drink groups. But mixing can make several real problems more likely.

### You lose track of how much you've had

This is the big one. A pint of beer, a glass of wine, a cocktail, and a shot all contain different amounts of alcohol, and they don't add up in an obvious way. A strong IPA or a large pour of wine can hold close to two standard drinks. Many cocktails contain two or more shots. When you hop between drink types, it's much harder to keep a mental count, and people tend to underestimate their total.

### Strengths vary more than you'd think

| Drink | Typical serving | Rough alcohol content |
|---|---|---|
| Regular beer (about 5%) | 12 oz / 355 ml | About 1 standard drink |
| Strong craft beer (7 to 9%) | 16 oz pint | About 2 standard drinks or more |
| Wine (about 12%) | 5 oz / 150 ml | About 1 standard drink |
| Large restaurant pour of wine | 8 to 9 oz | About 1.5 to 2 standard drinks |
| Spirits (40%) | 1.5 oz / 44 ml shot | About 1 standard drink |
| Mixed cocktail | Varies | Often 1.5 to 3 standard drinks |

In the US, a standard drink contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. The figures above are rounded and vary by brand and pour. The point is simple: if you're switching between drinks like these, "I had five drinks" can easily mean eight or nine standard drinks.

### Fizzy drinks may speed absorption

Some small studies suggest that alcohol mixed with carbonated mixers can reach the bloodstream faster than the same alcohol served flat, likely because carbonation speeds the movement of alcohol from the stomach into the small intestine, where it's absorbed quickly. The effect varies a lot between people. It's one reason a night of champagne, spritzes, or vodka sodas can hit harder than expected. Our guide to the [champagne hangover](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) covers this in more detail.

### Mixing alcohol with energy drinks is a separate problem

This isn't about mixing alcohol types, but it's often lumped in. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, which can mask how impaired you are and lead some people to drink more. Public health agencies, including the CDC, have warned that combining alcohol with energy drinks is linked to heavier drinking and riskier behavior. Feeling awake is not the same as being sober.

### The verdict on mixing

Mixing beer, wine, and spirits in one evening isn't chemically dangerous for a healthy adult in moderate amounts. The practical risk is that it often leads to drinking more, and faster, than you realize. If you mix, count standard drinks honestly.

## What Actually Causes Hangovers

If order doesn't matter, what does? Hangovers have several overlapping causes, and research is still filling in the picture. Here are the main ones, roughly in order of importance.

### 1. Total alcohol (by far the biggest factor)

The amount of ethanol you drink is the strongest single predictor of how bad a hangover will be. Above a certain level, almost everyone gets one. Ethanol disrupts sleep, irritates the stomach, triggers inflammation, affects blood sugar, and is broken down into **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound that your body then has to clear. A broader look at why this happens is in our guide on [how to cure a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-cure-a-hangover-complete-science-guide).

### 2. How fast you drink

Your liver can only process alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, roughly one standard drink an hour for many adults (it varies with body size, sex, genetics, and other factors). Drinking faster than that doesn't speed up the liver. It just raises the level of alcohol in your blood and keeps it high for longer. That's why the "beer then rapid shots" pattern from the pace theory leads to such bad mornings.

### 3. Congeners

Congeners are the natural by-products of fermentation and aging that give drinks much of their flavor, aroma, and color. They include small amounts of methanol, other alcohols (sometimes called fusel oils), acetaldehyde, tannins, and many other compounds. Dark, aged, or fruit-based drinks tend to contain more of them than clear, highly filtered ones.

Roughly speaking, drinks tend to fall like this:

- **Higher in congeners:** brandy, bourbon and other whiskies, dark rum, red wine, tequila that isn't 100% agave
- **Middle:** white wine, most beers
- **Lower in congeners:** vodka, gin, clear rum, and other highly filtered clear spirits

The best-known test is a study by Damaris Rohsenow and colleagues published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010. Young adults drank to the same breath-alcohol level on bourbon (high in congeners), on vodka (low in congeners), or on a placebo. Hangovers were worse after bourbon than after vodka. But here's the important part: next-day impairment on tasks like attention and reaction time was similar after both. In other words, congeners made people *feel* worse, but the alcohol itself was what impaired them.

This is the real science that the beer-before-liquor rhyme sort of gestures at. If your night includes a lot of dark liquor or red wine, you may feel worse than after the same amount of alcohol from vodka or light beer. But that's about the *type* of drink, not the *order*. You can read drink-specific breakdowns in our guides to the [whiskey hangover](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), the [vodka hangover](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), and the [wine hangover](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide).

### 4. Specific compounds in specific drinks

Some drinks carry their own extra suspects. Red wine is a good example. Researchers at UC Davis reported in 2023 that quercetin, a natural plant compound in red wine grapes, can be converted in the body into a form that may interfere with the breakdown of acetaldehyde, which might explain why some people get headaches from even small amounts of red wine. That work was based on lab findings and needs confirmation in people, but it shows that drink-specific effects are real, and that they have nothing to do with drinking order. For more on alcohol headaches specifically, see our guide on [why alcohol causes headaches](/never-hungover/alcohol-headache-why-it-happens-how-to-prevent-2025).

### 5. Dehydration, poor sleep, and an empty stomach

Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin) that helps your kidneys hold onto water, so you urinate more. It also fragments sleep, especially in the second half of the night. Drinking on an empty stomach lets alcohol absorb faster. None of these alone fully explains a hangover (research has found that hangover severity doesn't line up neatly with markers of dehydration), but they all make it worse.

### 6. Your own body

People vary a lot in how sensitive they are to hangovers. Genetics, body weight, sex, age, and drinking history all play a part. Some people report almost never getting hangovers even after heavy drinking, while others feel rough after a few drinks. That's another reason to judge by your own experience and your own limits, not a rhyme.

## How to Actually Reduce Your Chances of a Hangover

These steps have much better support than drink order. Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes into more detail.

1. **Set a number before you go out.** Decide how many standard drinks you'll have and stick to it. This is the single most effective thing you can do.
2. **Pace yourself.** Aim for about one standard drink an hour or slower, especially later in the evening, which is exactly when the "beer then shots" pattern tends to speed things up.
3. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between alcoholic drinks slows your pace and helps with fluid loss.
4. **Eat first, and keep eating.** A meal with protein, fat, and carbohydrate slows how quickly alcohol enters your bloodstream.
5. **Choose lower-congener drinks if you're hangover-prone.** Clear spirits with non-sugary mixers, or lighter beers and white wines, may leave you feeling better than the same amount of alcohol from bourbon, brandy, or red wine.
6. **Be wary of strong, sweet, or fizzy drinks.** They're easy to drink fast and can hide how much alcohol you're getting.
7. **Watch your pours.** Home pours and restaurant wine glasses are often much larger than a standard drink.
8. **Protect your sleep.** Stop drinking a few hours before bed if you can, so your body has time to process some of the alcohol first.
9. **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Drinking more in the morning only delays the hangover.

If you're already hungover, rest, fluids, food, and time are the main tools. Be careful with painkillers after drinking. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and alcohol both put work on the liver, and ibuprofen-type drugs can irritate a stomach already irritated by alcohol. Read the label, stick to the dose, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

## Where Supplements Like DHM Fit (Honestly)

Some people add supplements to their routine. The most researched of these on our site is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, which suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and may support the liver. Human evidence is limited, and DHM is not a proven hangover cure. It does not change the fact that total alcohol is the main driver of a hangover, and it won't make heavy drinking safe.

If you'd like to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Treat any supplement as a small extra on top of the basics above, not a replacement for them.

## Other Drinking Myths in the Same Family

The beer-before-liquor rhyme has plenty of company. A few quick checks:

- **"Clear liquor never gives you a hangover."** False. Clear spirits tend to have fewer congeners, so they may cause somewhat milder hangovers at the same dose, but enough vodka will still give you a bad one.
- **"Expensive alcohol doesn't cause hangovers."** Mostly false. Price doesn't decide congener content or alcohol strength. Some premium spirits are aged and high in congeners.
- **"You can sweat or run off a hangover."** Not really. Exercise won't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, and it can add to dehydration.
- **"Coffee sobers you up."** No. Caffeine can make you feel more alert, but your blood alcohol level is unchanged.
- **"Throwing up makes you less drunk."** Unreliable. Most alcohol is absorbed fairly quickly, and vomiting is a sign you've had too much, which is why it was linked to worse hangovers in the 2019 trial.

## The Bottom Line

- The order you drink in (beer before liquor, liquor before beer, wine before beer) does not meaningfully change your hangover, according to the best controlled study on the question.
- Total alcohol and how fast you drink it are the biggest drivers of a hangover. Congeners, found in higher amounts in dark and aged drinks, can make it somewhat worse.
- The saying probably survives because the order often tracks how fast people drink. Speeding up with strong drinks late in the night is the real problem.
- Mixing drink types isn't harmful by itself, but it makes it easier to lose count. Count standard drinks honestly.
- Pace, water, food, and a set limit will do far more for your morning than any rhyme.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is "beer before liquor, never been sicker" true?**

No. A 2019 randomized crossover trial from Witten/Herdecke University, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, found that the order of drinks made no significant difference to hangover severity once the total amount of alcohol was controlled. The amount and speed of drinking matter far more than the sequence.

**Does mixing alcohol make you sicker?**

Not by itself. In the 2019 trial, people who mixed beer and wine had hangovers similar to those who drank only one. The real risk of mixing is practical: different drinks have very different strengths, so it's easy to lose track and drink more than you realize, which does lead to worse hangovers.

**Where did the saying "liquor before beer, you're in the clear" come from?**

Nobody knows its exact origin, and similar rhymes exist in German and other languages. The most convincing explanation is about pace: starting with weak beer and switching to strong liquor late in the night, when judgment is already impaired, tends to mean drinking a lot of alcohol very quickly. The order is a marker of heavy, fast drinking, not the cause of the hangover.

**What actually causes a hangover?**

The biggest factor is how much alcohol you drink and how fast. Alcohol disrupts sleep, irritates the stomach, triggers inflammation, increases urination, and is broken down into a toxic compound called acetaldehyde. Congeners, the by-products of fermentation and aging found in larger amounts in dark drinks like bourbon, brandy, and red wine, can make hangovers worse. Individual genetics and drinking on an empty stomach also play a part.

**Are dark liquors worse for hangovers than clear ones?**

Often, yes, at the same amount of alcohol. A 2010 study in Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research found that hangovers were worse after bourbon than after vodka at the same breath-alcohol level, likely because bourbon contains more congeners. However, next-day impairment was similar, so clear spirits are not a safe way to drink more.

**Did the beer-before-liquor study actually test liquor?**

No. The 2019 trial tested beer and white wine, not spirits. Its title referenced the saying "grape or grain but never the twain." However, there's no known biological reason why the order of beer and liquor would matter when the order of beer and wine doesn't, since your body processes the alcohol in each the same way. Drink type can matter because of congeners, but that's independent of order.

**What's the best order to drink in to avoid a hangover?**

There isn't one. Instead of planning an order, set a limit in standard drinks, pace yourself at about one drink an hour or slower, alternate with water, and eat before and while drinking. If you're prone to bad hangovers, choosing lower-congener drinks such as clear spirits or lighter beers may help a little.

**Can a supplement like DHM let me ignore these rules?**

No. DHM has promising research, mostly from animal and lab studies, but limited human evidence. It isn't a proven hangover cure and doesn't change the fact that total alcohol drives hangovers. If you try it, treat it as a small extra on top of drinking less, drinking slower, eating, and staying hydrated.
